title: The statmodels7 Framework
text:
Preface
This book is the mathematical companion to the statmodels7 toolkit. Its purpose is to collect in one place, with complete derivations, the mathematics that the packages implement: the link functions with their derivatives to fourth order, the probability distributions with their scores and information matrices, and the operations that build new distributions out of existing ones — changes of variables, zero-inflation, zero-adjustment, truncation.
The style of the book follows a single rule: nothing is cited away. Whenever a formula appears, the derivation that produces it from the definitions appears with it, with the intermediate steps written out. A reader who wants to know why the score of a truncated distribution is the parent’s score recentred at its truncated mean, or why the expected information on the link scale is a simple congruence transform while the observed one is not, will find the argument on the page rather than a reference to it. The mathematics is elementary throughout — calculus, a little probability, the occasional exchange of derivative and integral — and the aim has been to make every step easy to follow, so that the book can be read as a course in the likelihood theory of parametric families as much as a description of one particular software toolkit.
The book is generated with Quarto directly from the source code of the packages, which are loaded from the working tree each time it is rendered. The numerical examples scattered through the chapters are therefore executed by the very code they illustrate, and the output shown is the output produced at build time.

title: The statmodels7 Framework
text:
How the book is organised
After the introduction there is one chapter per package, so that the book grows the way the toolkit does.
1  Introduction explains what the toolkit is for and why it is built the way it is. It contains no mathematics and can be read on its own.
2  The linkfunctions7 package is linkfunctions7: what a link is required to satisfy, how the derivatives of a link and of its inverse determine one another, and why they are carried to fourth order. It ends with a catalogue of the sixteen link classes, each with its formulas written out in full.
3  The distributions7 package is distributions7, and divides into four. Distributions develops the likelihood theory the toolkit rests on — score, observed and expected information, the Bartlett identities, derivatives on the unconstrained scale via Faà di Bruno’s formula, derivatives of the distribution function — and presents the fourteen families, with particular care where the parametrisation differs from the one base R uses. Transformations of distributions treats the operations that turn one distribution into another, and is the most demanding part of the book: the wrappers compose with any parent, so their formulas are derived once, in general, and every one of them is proved. Fitting a distribution fits a distribution to a sample by maximum likelihood, which is the smallest problem that exercises all of the preceding machinery at once. What a distribution gets for free describes what a distribution receives when it implements nothing but its density.
Appendix A — Notation collects the notation used throughout.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 One Gamma, written many times
Open almost any R modelling package and somewhere in its internals you will find a Gamma distribution — not the Gamma distribution, but that package’s own private copy of it, written as a handful of helper functions: a switch on a character string that returns a density, a closure that computes a score, a block inside a fitting routine that produces whatever second derivative the routine happens to need. The same is true of link functions. Every package that fits something positive carries its own log link, and every package that fits a probability carries its own logit.
None of these objects can be reused, because none of them is really an object. They are code paths, private to the package that owns them, and they contain only what their author’s routine happened to call for — usually the density and the score, sometimes the Hessian, almost never anything beyond. A package that needs a third derivative writes its own Gamma from scratch; a package that wants derivatives with respect to an unconstrained parameter does the same. The result is that the R ecosystem contains dozens of Gamma distributions, each partial, each written under deadline, and each capable of being wrong in its own way.
The observation the toolkit is built on is that all of this is unnecessary, because a Gamma distribution is a fixed mathematical object. It does not vary from package to package. Its density, its score, its information, its third and fourth derivatives, its derivatives with respect to the response, its behaviour under any reparametrisation — all of these are determined once and for all by the definition, and they can therefore be written down once, correctly and completely, for everyone to build on.
That is what statmodels7 is: infrastructure meant to be reused, rather than another modelling package. The measure of its success is not how well it fits models but whether somebody else’s modelling package can be built on top of it.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 What “completely” means
The principle applies to both kinds of object the toolkit currently provides, and it is worth stating for each, because what counts as complete differs.
A link function is a map between a constrained parameter and an unconstrained one, and what a modelling routine can ask of it is its value and its derivatives — in both directions. Almost every implementation in R carries the first derivative of the inverse link and stops there, which is exactly what a GLM fitted by iterative least squares needs and nothing more. A link in this toolkit carries four derivatives of the forward map and four of the inverse, so that it can serve a routine working to any order up to the fourth, and it knows its own domain so that the routine does not have to.
A distribution supplies, or can derive, the density or mass function together with the cdf, the quantile function and a random generator; the score and the observed information; the expected information; third and fourth derivatives of the log-likelihood, both observed and expected; derivatives with respect to the response as well as the parameters; derivatives of the distribution function, which is what a censored observation contributes; and every one of these with respect to the unconstrained parameters as well as the natural ones.
The items at the end of each list are the ones usually missing elsewhere, and they are precisely the ones a modelling framework depends on. Derivatives in the response are what quantile-type residuals and smoothness penalties are made of. Derivatives on the unconstrained scale are what an optimiser wants: a Gamma variance must stay positive, and an algorithm forced to respect that constraint is doing constrained optimisation, whereas an algorithm working with \(\eta = \log \sigma^2\) moves freely over the whole real line. Third and fourth derivatives, finally, are the raw material of higher-order asymptotics and bias correction.
This is also where the two packages meet, and why neither would be much use alone. Transporting a fourth derivative of a log-likelihood from the natural scale to the unconstrained one is an application of Faà di Bruno’s formula, and it consumes exactly the four derivatives of the inverse link that linkfunctions7 carries — Section 3.1.4 works this out in detail. A link stopping at second order would silently cap the whole toolkit at second-order methods, however much the distributions knew about themselves.

The destination is the last row: a framework in the spirit of GAMLSS in which every parameter of a distribution can be modelled rather than just the mean, the optimiser is pluggable, estimation can be frequentist or Bayesian, and users can define new model terms and drop them straight into formulas. Everything below it exists to make that possible, and one design pressure has shaped it all: exact derivatives, on the unconstrained scale, for components the framework has never seen before.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Extension is the point
A toolkit that worked only for the sixteen links and fourteen distributions it ships with would have solved nothing; it would simply be one more closed catalogue, larger than the others. What matters is what happens when a user brings an object the authors never considered, and in both packages the answer is that it is treated exactly like the ones that came with them — there is no registration step, and no separate interface for the “advanced” case.
For a link the requirement is only that the ten generics be implemented, and since a link is a formula and its derivatives, that is a dozen lines. Nothing distinguishes the result from a built-in one: it can be handed to any distribution as the link for any parameter, and the fourth-order machinery will use it without knowing where it came from.

NegLog <- S7::new_class("NegLog", parent = link, package = NULL)

S7::method(linkfun,   NegLog) <- function(x, theta) -log(theta)
S7::method(linkinv,   NegLog) <- function(x, eta)   exp(-eta)
S7::method(dlinkfun,  NegLog) <- function(x, theta) -1 / theta
S7::method(d2linkfun, NegLog) <- function(x, theta)  1 / theta^2
S7::method(dlinkinv,  NegLog) <- function(x, eta)   -exp(-eta)
S7::method(d2linkinv, NegLog) <- function(x, eta)    exp(-eta)

neglog <- NegLog(link_name = "neglog", link_bounds = c(0, Inf), link_params = NULL)
linkinv(neglog, linkfun(neglog, c(0.5, 2)))
#> [1] 0.5 2.0

For a distribution the contract is even smaller, and it is the one that decides whether the package is infrastructure or a catalogue: a new distribution needs nothing but its density. Everything else has a fallback — the cdf is computed by quadrature, the quantile function by root-finding, the random generator by a ratio-of-uniforms scheme that needs only the density, and every derivative by finite differences. Whatever the user later supplies in closed form simply replaces the corresponding fallback, with no registration step and no separate interface for the “advanced” case.
To see what this means in practice, here is a complete definition of the Rayleigh distribution, which has density \(f(y;\sigma) = (y/\sigma^2)\, e^{-y^2/2\sigma^2}\) on \((0, \infty)\):

Rayleigh <- S7::new_class("Rayleigh", parent = continuous_distrib, package = NULL)

S7::method(distrib_pdf, Rayleigh) <- function(distrib, y, theta, log = FALSE) {
  s <- theta[[1]]
  ld <- log(y) - 2 * log(s) - y^2 / (2 * s^2)
  if (log) ld else exp(ld)
}

rayleigh <- Rayleigh(
  distrib_name = "rayleigh", dimension = "univariate", bounds = c(0, Inf),
  params = "sigma", params_interpretation = c(sigma = "scale"), n_params = 1,
  params_bounds = list(sigma = c(0, Inf)),
  link_params = list(sigma = log_link())
)

Nothing above mentions a cdf, a quantile function, a generator or a derivative, and yet all of them are immediately available. The median of a Rayleigh is \(\sigma\sqrt{2\log 2}\), its score is \(y^2/\sigma^3 - 2/\sigma\), and its expected information is \(4/\sigma^2\); the fallbacks recover each of these from the density alone:

theta <- list(sigma = 2)

distrib_quantile(rayleigh, 0.5, theta)     # by root-finding on the numerical cdf
#> [1] 2.35482
2 * sqrt(2 * log(2))                       # the closed form
#> [1] 2.35482

distrib_gradient(rayleigh, c(1, 3), theta) # by finite differences
#> $sigma
#> [1] -0.875  0.125
c(1, 3)^2 / 2^3 - 2 / 2                    # the closed form
#> [1] -0.875  0.125

distrib_expected_hessian(rayleigh, 1, theta)$sigma_sigma   # -4/sigma^2
#> [1] -1

The twenty lines above are a first-class citizen of the toolkit: the object can be zero-inflated, truncated, transformed, and fitted by Fisher scoring exactly like the distributions the package ships with.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Checking one’s own work
Because users are expected to write their own distributions and links, the packages ship the tools to validate them. check_link() verifies that a link is invertible in both directions, strictly monotone, consistent with the inverse function theorem, and that each analytical derivative agrees with a numerical one; check_distrib() runs the analogous battery on a distribution — the density integrates to one, the cdf and the quantile function invert each other and agree with the density, the random generator matches the cdf, every derivative matches a finite-difference computation, and the expected information matches a Monte Carlo estimate of the variance of the score.
Both run on any object, including one written five minutes ago — here, on the two defined above:

invisible(check_link(neglog))
#> Checking S7 Link Object: neglog 
#>   [1] Invertibility (Theta space): [PASSED] 
#>   [2] Invertibility (Eta space):   [PASSED] 
#>   [3] Strict Monotonicity:         [PASSED] 
#>   [4] Inverse Function Theorem:    [PASSED] 
#>   [5] Link Derivatives:            [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical] 
#>   [6] Inverse Link Derivatives:    [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical]


res <- check_distrib(rayleigh, theta = list(sigma = 2), orders = 1:2,
                     nsim = 5e4, verbose = FALSE)
res[, c("check", "status")]
#>                                         check status
#> 1                     density integrates to 1     OK
#> 2                     density is non-negative     OK
#> 3             cdf in [0,1] and non-decreasing     OK
#> 4                 cdf agrees with the density     OK
#> 5                     quantile/cdf round-trip     OK
#> 6                         rng matches the cdf     OK
#> 7              gradient vs finite differences     OK
#> 8               hessian vs finite differences     OK
#> 9         expected information vs Monte Carlo     OK
#> 10 response derivatives vs finite differences     OK
#> 11  link-scale gradient vs finite differences     OK

The link above declares only two derivative orders of the four, and the validator says so rather than passing what it was not given.
They are used systematically on everything the packages contain. The three chapters that follow present the mathematics behind all of it, one per package: Chapter 2 for linkfunctions7, Chapter 3 for distributions7, and Chapter 4 for optimizers7.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.1 What a link function is
The parameters of a distribution rarely live on the whole real line. A scale must be positive, a probability lies between zero and one, a correlation between minus one and one. An optimiser, on the other hand, is happiest with an argument it can move freely in any direction. A link function is the bridge between the two worlds: it maps the natural, constrained domain of a parameter onto an unconstrained scale, and its inverse maps the optimiser’s iterates back into the domain where the distribution makes sense. This chapter defines the objects precisely, works out the relationship between the derivatives of a link and those of its inverse, explains why the toolkit carries both to fourth order, and ends with the full catalogue of the sixteen link classes that linkfunctions7 provides.
Each clause of this definition is a decision with consequences, so it is worth pausing on all three.
Notice first what the definition does not say: it never asks \(g\) to be increasing. Monotonicity is a consequence rather than an assumption — a continuous function whose derivative never vanishes on an interval cannot change the sign of that derivative, so it is automatically strictly monotone — but the direction is left free, and this freedom is used. The link for a parameter bounded above, \(g(\theta) = \log(u - \theta)\), is strictly decreasing, and it is a perfectly good link. Code that quietly assumes an increasing link, for instance when mapping quantiles through it, breaks on exactly that case, which is why the natural property to require, and to test, is strict monotonicity of either sign.
Second, the image \(E\) need not be the whole real line. For the square-root link \(E = (0, \infty)\), and for the reciprocal link it is a half-line as well. In such cases the optimiser is not truly unconstrained — the constraint has merely moved from \(\theta\) to \(\eta\) — and it helps to know this in advance, because these are the links where an optimiser can step outside the domain and come back with NaN. The catalogue below therefore states \(E\) explicitly for every link.
Third, and most characteristically for this toolkit, the definition demands four continuous derivatives rather than the customary one or two. The link objects in stats::make.link() carry the first derivative of the inverse and nothing else, which is all a GLM fitted by IRLS ever needs. Here the ambitions are higher: as Section 3.1.4 will show in detail, transporting a fourth-order derivative of a log-likelihood onto the unconstrained scale requires \(h'\), \(h''\), \(h'''\) and \(h''''\), so a link that stopped at second order would silently cap the entire toolkit at second-order methods.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text: Definition 2.1 (Link function) Let \(\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be an open interval. A link function on \(\Theta\) is a map \(g : \Theta \to \mathbb{R}\) which is a bijection onto its image \(E = g(\Theta)\), itself an open interval; which is four times continuously differentiable on \(\Theta\); and which is regular, meaning that \(g'(\theta) \neq 0\) everywhere. We write \(h = g^{-1} : E \to \Theta\) for the inverse, and throughout the book \(\eta = g(\theta)\) and \(\theta = h(\eta)\).

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
section: 2.2 The derivatives of an inverse function
text:
2.2 The derivatives of an inverse function
Every link in the catalogue implements two families of derivatives: those of \(g\) with respect to \(\theta\), and those of \(h\) with respect to \(\eta\). The two families are not independent — each determines the other completely — and the relationship between them is worth deriving carefully, both because the formulas are used throughout the toolkit and because the derivation is a pleasant exercise in the disciplined use of the chain rule.

Theorem 2.1 (Derivatives of an inverse function) Let \(g\) be a link function in the sense of Definition 2.1 and let \(h = g^{-1}\). Then, with every derivative of \(g\) evaluated at \(\theta = h(\eta)\),
\[
h' = \frac{1}{g'}, \qquad
h'' = -\frac{g''}{(g')^{3}}, \qquad
h''' = \frac{3(g'')^{2} - g'g'''}{(g')^{5}}, \qquad
h'''' = \frac{-15(g'')^{3} + 10\,g'g''g''' - (g')^{2}g''''}{(g')^{7}}.
\]


Proof. The whole argument flows from one identity. Since \(h\) undoes \(g\), we have \(h(g(\theta)) = \theta\) for every \(\theta\) in the domain, and we may differentiate this identity as many times as we like; each differentiation yields a relation between the derivatives of \(h\) and those of \(g\), from which the next unknown derivative of \(h\) can be isolated. Throughout, \(h^{(k)}\) is shorthand for \(h^{(k)}(g(\theta))\).
Differentiating once, the chain rule gives \(h'\,g' = 1\). Since \(g'\) never vanishes, we may divide by it, and the first formula, \(h' = 1/g'\), is already in hand.
Now differentiate \(h'g' = 1\) again. The left side is a product whose two factors both depend on \(\theta\) — the first through the composition with \(g\) — so the product rule together with the chain rule gives
\[h''\,(g')^{2} + h'\,g'' = 0 .\]
Solving for \(h''\) and substituting \(h' = 1/g'\),
\[h'' = -\frac{h'\,g''}{(g')^{2}} = -\frac{g''}{(g')^{3}},\]
which is the second formula. Note the pattern that will repeat: each new differentiation produces an equation that is linear in the highest derivative of \(h\), with coefficient a power of \(g'\), so isolating it is always a division.
Differentiating \(h''(g')^{2} + h'g'' = 0\) once more, and collecting the terms carefully,
\[h'''\,(g')^{3} + 3\,h''\,g'\,g'' + h'\,g''' = 0 . \tag{$\ast$}\]
Substituting the expressions already obtained for \(h''\) and \(h'\), the middle term becomes \(-3(g'')^{2}/(g')^{2}\) and the last becomes \(g'''/g'\), so that
\[h''' = -\frac{1}{(g')^{3}}\left(-\frac{3(g'')^{2}}{(g')^{2}} + \frac{g'''}{g'}\right)
       = \frac{3(g'')^{2} - g'\,g'''}{(g')^{5}} .\]
One more round. Differentiating each of the three terms of \((\ast)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{d\theta}\!\left[h'''(g')^{3}\right] &= h''''(g')^{4} + 3h'''(g')^{2}g'', \\
\frac{d}{d\theta}\!\left[3h''g'g''\right] &= 3h'''(g')^{2}g'' + 3h''(g'')^{2} + 3h''g'g''', \\
\frac{d}{d\theta}\!\left[h'g'''\right] &= h''g'g''' + h'g'''' ,
\end{aligned}
\]
and adding the three lines and setting the sum to zero,
\[h''''(g')^{4} + 6h'''(g')^{2}g'' + 3h''(g'')^{2} + 4h''g'g''' + h'g'''' = 0 .\]
It remains to substitute the three lower-order results and simplify. Putting everything except the first term over the common denominator \((g')^{3}\), the sum of the known terms works out to
\[\frac{15(g'')^{3} - 10\,g'g''g''' + (g')^{2}g''''}{(g')^{3}},\]
and dividing by \(-(g')^{4}\) yields the stated expression for \(h''''\). \(\square\)

A quick example makes the formulas concrete, and catches sign errors better than any amount of staring. Take the log link, \(g(\theta) = \log\theta\), whose inverse \(h(\eta) = e^\eta\) has the agreeable property of being its own derivative to every order, so every \(h^{(k)}\) should equal \(u = e^{\eta} = \theta\). On the forward side \(g' = u^{-1}\), \(g'' = -u^{-2}\), \(g''' = 2u^{-3}\) and \(g'''' = -6u^{-4}\). Feeding these into the fourth formula,
\[\frac{-15(-u^{-2})^{3} + 10\,u^{-1}(-u^{-2})(2u^{-3}) - u^{-2}(-6u^{-4})}{u^{-7}}
= \frac{15u^{-6} - 20u^{-6} + 6u^{-6}}{u^{-7}} = u,\]
exactly as it should.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.3 Why the fourth order matters
It is fair to ask whether a fourth derivative of a link function is ever really used, or whether it is completeness for its own sake. The answer comes from the formula that will be derived in Section 3.1.4 for the fourth derivative of a log-likelihood with respect to the linear predictor:
\[
\frac{\partial^{4}\ell}{\partial\eta^{4}}
= \ell^{(\theta\theta\theta\theta)}(h')^{4}
+ 6\,\ell^{(\theta\theta\theta)}(h')^{2}h''
+ \ell^{(\theta\theta)}\left(4h'h''' + 3(h'')^{2}\right)
+ \ell^{(\theta)}\,h'''' .
\]
The last term contains \(h''''\), and it does not vanish for any link except an affine one. A link truncated at second order would therefore not merely make this quantity less accurate — it would make it wrong, by an amount that has nothing to do with any small parameter and does not shrink as the sample grows. Since fourth-order likelihood derivatives are exactly what bias correction and higher-order asymptotics consume, the four-derivative requirement in Definition 2.1 is a load-bearing part of the design.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.4 The interface
A link is an S7 object. The base class link carries the name, the domain \(\Theta\) (link_bounds), and any extra mathematical parameters the link needs, such as the exponent of the power link; each concrete link is a subclass.

lk <- logit_link()
lk
#> S7 Link Object: logit
#>   - Parameter domain (theta): (0, 1)
c(lk@link_name, lk@link_bounds)
#> [1] "logit" "0"     "1"

Every link implements the same ten generics, five in each direction:

The ten generics


Generic
Returns




linkfun(x, theta)
\(g(\theta)\)


linkinv(x, eta)
\(h(\eta)\)


dlinkfun … d4linkfun
\(g'(\theta)\) … \(g''''(\theta)\)


dlinkinv … d4linkinv
\(h'(\eta)\) … \(h''''(\eta)\)



For interactive work, two routers select the order at run time:

theta <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
linkfun(lk, theta)
#> [1] -1.386294  0.000000  1.386294
linkderiv(lk, theta, order = 2)
#> [1] -23.4375   0.0000  23.4375
linkinvderiv(lk, linkfun(lk, theta), order = 2)
#> [1]  0.096  0.000 -0.096

One practical remark about these routers. linkderiv() dispatches on the link and then calls the order-specific generic, which dispatches again; since an S7 dispatch costs roughly five microseconds against one for a plain call, the second dispatch accounts for about a third of the total. In a hot loop this adds up — distributions7 evaluates inverse-link derivatives once per parameter per order on every scoring iteration — so performance-critical code calls dlinkinv() and its siblings directly, and the routers are best regarded as a convenience for interactive use.

logit_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, 1)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \log\dfrac{\theta}{1-\theta}, \qquad h(\eta) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}} \equiv p\]

Splitting \(g' = \theta^{-1} + (1-\theta)^{-1}\) makes the higher orders immediate: \(g^{(k)} = (-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\,\theta^{-k} + (k-1)!\,(1-\theta)^{-k}\). On the inverse side every derivative is a polynomial in \(p\) times \(p(1-p)\); the coefficients \(1, -2, (1,-6,6), (1,-14,36,-24)\) are the Eulerian-type numbers generated by \(\partial_\eta\) acting on \(p(1-p)\).

probit_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, 1)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \Phi^{-1}(\theta), \qquad h(\eta) = \Phi(\eta)\]

Probit: derivatives to fourth order







\(k\)
\(g^{(k)}(\theta)\)
\(h^{(k)}(\eta)\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\varphi(z)}\)
\(\varphi(\eta)\)

\(\dfrac{1+2z^{2}}{\varphi(z)^{3}}\)

The inverse derivatives are the probabilists’ Hermite polynomials: \(h^{(k)}(\eta) = (-1)^{k-1}He_{k-1}(\eta)\varphi(\eta)\) with \(He_0 = 1\), \(He_1 = \eta\), \(He_2 = \eta^{2}-1\), \(He_3 = \eta^{3}-3\eta\). In the forward direction there is no closed form free of \(\Phi^{-1}\), so the implementation evaluates \(z = \Phi^{-1}(\theta)\) once and writes everything in terms of \(z\) and \(\varphi(z)\).


2.5.8 Complementary log-log
cloglog_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, 1)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \log\!\left(-\log(1-\theta)\right), \qquad h(\eta) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-e^{\eta}\right)\]

\(g^{(k)}(\theta)\)
\(h^{(k)}(\eta)\)

\(-\dfrac{1}{vL}\)

Here \(v = 1-\theta\), \(L = \log v < 0\) and \(z = e^{\eta}\). The asymmetric link of the extreme-value family. The implementation evaluates the inverse derivatives as \(\sum_k c_k \exp(k\eta - z)\) rather than in the factored form \((\cdot)\,e^{-z}\) shown above: for large \(\eta\) the factored form computes \(\infty \times 0\) and returns NaN, whereas the combined exponent underflows cleanly to zero. Wherever both are finite the two forms are algebraically identical.

loglog_link()

With \(l = \log\theta < 0\) and \(z = e^{-\eta}\). The mirror image of the complementary log-log: \(g_{\mathrm{loglog}}(\theta) =

cauchit_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, 1)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \tan\!\left(\pi(\theta - \tfrac{1}{2})\right), \qquad h(\eta) = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{\pi}\arctan\eta\]

With \(z = g(\theta)\). The heavy-tailed alternative to probit: the inverse is the Cauchy cdf, so \(h'\) is the Cauchy density and the higher derivatives are its successive derivatives. Because \(h'\) decays only like \(\eta^{-2}\), an extreme linear predictor still moves the probability, which is the point of choosing it.


2.5.11 Rhobit (Fisher’s z)
rhobit_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (-1, 1)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).

The link for a correlation. It is the logit of \((\theta+1)/2\) up to a factor of two, which is why the inverse derivatives are the logistic ones rewritten in \(t = 2p-1\).


2.5.12 Power
power_link(lambda = 1.5)
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, \infty)\), so that \(\eta \in (0, \infty)\).

Shown at \(\lambda = 1.5\); \(k = 1/\lambda\) throughout. The falling factorial makes every order a one-liner. Note the trap this family sets in R: when \(\lambda = 2\) the second derivative is the constant \(\lambda(\lambda-1)\theta^{0}\), and NA^0 evaluates to 1, so a missing parameter would silently become a number. The package propagates missingness explicitly through na_from().


2.5.13 Softplus
softplus_link(a = 1)

\[g(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{a}\log\!\left(e^{a\theta}-1\right), \qquad h(\eta) = \tfrac{1}{a}\log\!\left(1+e^{a\eta}\right)\]

\(p\)

The inverse derivatives are the logistic ones scaled by \(a^{k-1}\). The forward ones are not evaluated in \(v\): it overflows once \(a\theta\) passes about \(709\), and since the derivatives divide by \(v^{k}\) the higher orders fail well before that. Writing \(\log v = a\theta + \log\!\left(1-e^{-a\theta}\right)\) and dividing each derivative through by the matching power of \(e^{a\theta}\) expresses everything in \(u = 1-e^{-a\theta} \in (0,1)\) instead, which is bounded for every \(\theta\); the two forms are algebraically identical wherever both are finite.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.6 Validating a link
Since users can define links of their own, the package provides check_link(), which takes any link object and verifies the properties that Definition 2.1 demands: invertibility in both directions on a grid, strict monotonicity of either sign, the first-order inverse function theorem \(h'(\eta)\,g'(\theta) = 1\), and the agreement of each analytical derivative, in both families and at every order up to the fourth, with a numerical one.

invisible(check_link(cloglog_link()))
#> Checking S7 Link Object: cloglog 
#>   [1] Invertibility (Theta space): [PASSED] 
#>   [2] Invertibility (Eta space):   [PASSED] 
#>   [3] Strict Monotonicity:         [PASSED] 
#>   [4] Inverse Function Theorem:    [PASSED] 
#>   [5] Link Derivatives:            [PASSED] 
#>   [6] Inverse Link Derivatives:    [PASSED]

The derivative checks are organised as a chain, and the reason deserves a paragraph, because it reflects a genuine limitation of numerical differentiation rather than an implementation detail. One cannot verify a fourth derivative by differentiating \(g\) itself four times numerically: each numerical differentiation amplifies the error of the previous one, and by the third order the result is noise. The validator instead compares the analytical derivative of order \(k\) against a single numerical differentiation of the analytical derivative of order \(k-1\), so that every comparison involves exactly one finite-difference step and retains its full accuracy. The grid, moreover, keeps away from the edges of the domain: the Richardson extrapolation in numDeriv evaluates the function at points up to about \(8 \times 10^{-4}\,|x|\) away from \(x\), and a grid point closer than that to a boundary would be differentiated using values from outside the domain.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
section: 2.7 What a link gets for free
text:
2.7 What a link gets for free
The ten generics of Section 2.4 are what a link may implement. Only two of them are compulsory. A link that supplies \(g\) and \(h\) and stops there still answers every derivative, because the base class carries numerical fallbacks for the eight it was not given, and the routers reach them like any other method.

BareLog <- S7::new_class("BareLog", parent = link, package = NULL)
S7::method(linkfun, BareLog) <- function(x, theta) log(theta)
S7::method(linkinv, BareLog) <- function(x, eta)   exp(eta)

bare <- BareLog(link_name = "bare log", link_bounds = c(0, Inf), link_params = NULL)

linkderiv(bare, 2, order = 3)   # third derivative, never written down
#> [1] 0.2500004
2 / 2^3                         # the closed form
#> [1] 0.25

This is the same bargain distributions7 offers a distribution that supplies only its density, and it exists for the same reason: the person most likely to need it is the one experimenting with a transformation nobody has implemented, and asking them to differentiate it by hand four times before anything runs is asking them not to bother.

2.7.1 One differentiation, never four
How a fallback computes its answer matters more here than one might expect, and the design follows the same rule Section 2.6 imposes on the validator: never differentiate numerically more than once in a row.
A fallback could be written recursively — the second derivative as a difference of the first, the third as a difference of the second — and it would be much the simplest thing to write. It would also be useless at the top, because each numerical differentiation multiplies the error of the one below it. The identity link makes the point with no arithmetic at all: its third derivative is exactly zero, and three nested differences return a number of order one.
What the fallbacks do instead is ask how many orders are actually missing. Each one finds the highest order \(m\) the link implements analytically, and applies a single central stencil of order \(k - m\) to that derivative:
\[
f' \approx \frac{f_{+1} - f_{-1}}{2h}, \qquad
f'' \approx \frac{f_{+1} - 2f_{0} + f_{-1}}{h^{2}},
\] \[
f''' \approx \frac{f_{+2} - 2f_{+1} + 2f_{-1} - f_{-2}}{2h^{3}}, \qquad
f'''' \approx \frac{f_{+2} - 4f_{+1} + 6f_{0} - 4f_{-1} + f_{-2}}{h^{4}},
\]
writing \(f_{\pm j}\) for \(f(x \pm jh)\). A link analytic to the second order therefore reaches the third with one difference and the fourth with two, rather than standing on three differences of its own — and the difference this makes is not marginal:

HalfLog <- S7::new_class("HalfLog", parent = link, package = NULL)
S7::method(linkfun,   HalfLog) <- function(x, theta) log(theta)
S7::method(linkinv,   HalfLog) <- function(x, eta)   exp(eta)
S7::method(dlinkfun,  HalfLog) <- function(x, theta) 1 / theta
S7::method(d2linkfun, HalfLog) <- function(x, theta) -1 / theta^2
S7::method(dlinkinv,  HalfLog) <- function(x, eta) exp(eta)
S7::method(d2linkinv, HalfLog) <- function(x, eta) exp(eta)

half <- HalfLog(link_name = "half log", link_bounds = c(0, Inf), link_params = NULL)

theta <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 5)
exact4 <- -6 / theta^4
rel <- function(a, b) max(abs(a - b) / abs(b))

c(nothing_analytic = rel(linkderiv(bare, theta, order = 4), exact4),
  two_orders_given = rel(linkderiv(half, theta, order = 4), exact4))
#> nothing_analytic two_orders_given 
#>     8.079000e-05     9.934107e-08

Two analytical orders, which is a couple of lines of algebra, buy several digits at the fourth. The step itself is \(\varepsilon^{1/(k+2)}\max(1, \lvert x\rvert)\) for a stencil of order \(k\), balancing truncation against rounding, and it is shrunk near the ends of the domain: a link’s domain is open, and the third- and fourth-order stencils reach \(2h\), so it is that reach and not \(h\) that has to fit inside it. Differentiating the log link at \(\theta = 10^{-8}\) would otherwise evaluate a logarithm at a negative number.


2.7.2 The catch, stated plainly
A convenience of this kind comes with a hazard, and it is the same one Section 3.4 records for distributions. check_link() verifies an analytical derivative by comparing it against a numerical one. If the analytical derivative is the numerical one, the comparison is between a quantity and itself: it agrees perfectly, and it has established nothing.
The validator therefore does not report such an order as passing. It reports it as numerical, and it says how far the exactness actually goes.

invisible(check_link(bare))
#> Checking S7 Link Object: bare log 
#>   [1] Invertibility (Theta space): [PASSED] 
#>   [2] Invertibility (Eta space):   [PASSED] 
#>   [3] Strict Monotonicity:         [PASSED] 
#>   [4] Inverse Function Theorem:    [PASSED] 
#>   [5] Link Derivatives:            [numerical] 
#>   [6] Inverse Link Derivatives:    [numerical]
invisible(check_link(half))
#> Checking S7 Link Object: half log 
#>   [1] Invertibility (Theta space): [PASSED] 
#>   [2] Invertibility (Eta space):   [PASSED] 
#>   [3] Strict Monotonicity:         [PASSED] 
#>   [4] Inverse Function Theorem:    [PASSED] 
#>   [5] Link Derivatives:            [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical] 
#>   [6] Inverse Link Derivatives:    [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical]

Neither link is wrong; both are simply less checked than a reader of a bare [PASSED] would assume, and the summary says so. link_fallback_orders() answers the same question programmatically, which is the form a script wants:

link_fallback_orders(half)
#> $forward
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $inverse
#> [1] 2
link_fallback_orders(logit_link())
#> $forward
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $inverse
#> [1] 4

Everything in the catalogue reports four and four. The fallbacks exist for links that do not yet, and the honest description of them is that they make an incomplete link usable rather than exact — which is why the catalogue does not rely on them, and why a link intended for serious use should end up not needing them either.

title: 3  The distributions7 package
text:
3.1 Distributions
Where Chapter 2 dealt with a transformation of a single number, this chapter deals with the object that transformation serves: a parametric family of probability distributions, carrying not only its density but everything a modelling routine might want to know about it.
The chapter is long because the package is, and it divides into four parts that can be read in order or dipped into. Section 3.1 sets out what a distrib object is obliged to provide and develops the likelihood theory the package rests on — score, observed and expected information, the Bartlett identities in full generality, derivatives transported onto the unconstrained scale by Faà di Bruno’s formula, derivatives with respect to the response, and derivatives of the distribution function that make censored likelihoods possible — before presenting the fourteen families themselves.
Section 3.2 turns to operators on distributions: a change of variables, zero-inflation, zero-adjustment and truncation, each of which takes a distribution and returns another one with all of the same machinery intact. The mathematics there is more interesting than it may sound, because the derivatives of the constructed model must be assembled from those of its parent, and doing that at fourth order in general requires a small amount of combinatorics.
Section 3.3 puts the apparatus to work on the simplest problem that exercises all of it, maximum likelihood for an i.i.d. sample, and Section 3.4 describes what a distribution receives when it implements nothing but its density — the part of the package that decides whether a family the author never anticipated is a first-class citizen or a second-class one.
This chapter develops the likelihood theory that the toolkit implements and then presents the fourteen distributions that distributions7 ships. The theory comes first because it is shared: the score, the two informations, the Bartlett identities and the change of scale are defined once, at the level of the base class, and every distribution — including one a user wrote this morning — inherits them. The catalogue comes second, with particular attention to the places where the parametrisation chosen here differs from the one base R uses, since those are the places where a reader is most likely to be surprised.
3.1.8 Gaussian
gaussian_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(y-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \sigma^{2}\]
The reference case: \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, as in dnorm(y, mu, sigma).


3.1.9 Cauchy
cauchy_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{1}{\pi\sigma\left[1 + \left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right]}\]
\[no moments exist\]
Neither the mean nor the variance exists, which is why check_distrib() validates the generator against the cdf rather than against the first two moments: a moment-based check would have nothing to compare here, and the cdf is both always available and the stronger claim.


3.1.10 Logistic
logistic_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{e^{-z}}{\sigma\left(1+e^{-z}\right)^{2}}, \qquad z = \frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \pi^{2}\sigma^{2}/3\]
Writing \(t = \sigma(z) = (1+e^{-z})^{-1}\) and \(u = 1-t\), the log-density is \(-\log\sigma + \log t + \log u\) and every observed derivative is a polynomial in \(t\): with \(g_1 = 1-2t\), \(g_2 = -2tu\), \(g_3 = g_2 g_1\), \(g_4 = g_2(1-6tu)\), the recursions \(\partial_\mu[A/\sigma^{k}] = -A'/\sigma^{k+1}\) and \(\partial_\sigma[A/\sigma^{k}] = -(zA' + kA)/\sigma^{k+1}\) generate all of them, overflow-free out to \(|z| = 4000\). The expected derivatives were rederived here because symbolic algebra systems return, for this family, expressions containing polylogarithms, the imaginary unit and a dependence on \(\mu\) — which is impossible for a location-scale family and is a useful reminder that a computer-algebra answer is not automatically a correct one. Seven of the nine expected third-order components are known exactly (\(\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\mu\mu\sigma}] = 1/(2\sigma^{3})\), \(\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\sigma\sigma\sigma}] = (\pi^{2}+2)/(2\sigma^{3})\), \(\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\mu^{4}}] = 1/(15\sigma^{4})\), the rest zero by symmetry); the two that remain require \(\int w^{k}\operatorname{sech}^{4}w\tanh^{2}w\,dw\) for \(k = 2, 4\) and are open. In the meantime approx = "integrate" supplies them to within Monte Carlo noise.


3.1.11 Student t
student_t_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sigma\sqrt{\nu\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)}\left(1+\frac{z^{2}}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}, \qquad z = \frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu\ (\nu>1), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \sigma^{2}\nu/(\nu-2)\ (\nu>2)\]
A location-scale family built on the standard \(t\): \(\sigma\) is a scale, not the standard deviation, which is \(\sigma\sqrt{\nu/(\nu-2)}\) and exists only for \(\nu > 2\). The degrees of freedom \(\nu\) are continuous and estimable.


3.1.12 Laplace
laplace_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{1}{2b}\exp\!\left\{-\frac{|y-\mu|}{b}\right\}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 2b^{2}\]
The one non-regular member of the catalogue: \(\ell\) has a kink at \(y = \mu\), the observed information in \(\mu\) is identically zero, and the Fisher information \(1/b^{2}\) can only be recovered from the score. See Section 3.1.22. params_smooth records this, and it is the reason that property exists at all.


3.1.13 Pseudo-Huber
pseudohuber_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[f(y) = \frac{\exp(-D)}{2\sigma\sqrt{\nu}\,K_{1}(\sqrt{\nu})}, \qquad D = \sqrt{\nu + \left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu; variance has no elementary closed form\]
The normalising constant is exact, not approximate: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\sqrt{a^{2}+z^{2}}}\,dz = 2aK_{1}(a)\), so with \(a = \sqrt{\nu}\) and \(dy = \sigma\,dz\) the constant is \(2\sigma\sqrt{\nu}K_{1}(\sqrt{\nu})\). The Bessel terms are degree-homogeneous, which is why the exponentially scaled besselK(x, nu, expon.scaled = TRUE) may be used: the scaling cancels between numerator and denominator, so it is exact rather than approximate, and it avoids overflow out to \(\nu = 2000\). \(\nu \to \infty\) gives a Gaussian limit and small \(\nu\) a Laplace-like one, so the family interpolates between the two — with, unlike the Laplace, a genuinely smooth log-density everywhere.


3.1.14 Gamma
gamma_distrib()
Support: \(y \in (0, \infty)\).
\[f(y) = \frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}y^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta y}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\mu^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}, \quad \beta = \frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \sigma^{2}\]
Not the base-R parametrisation. dgamma() takes a shape and a rate; this object takes the mean and the variance directly, which is what a modelling framework wants, since it is \(\mu\) that gets a linear predictor. The map is \(\alpha = \mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\), \(\beta = \mu/\sigma^{2}\), whence \(\alpha/\beta = \mu\) and \(\alpha/\beta^{2} = \sigma^{2}\) as claimed.


3.1.15 Inverse Gaussian
invgauss_distrib()
Support: \(y \in (0, \infty)\).
\[f(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\phi y^{3}}}\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(y-\mu)^{2}}{2\phi\mu^{2}y}\right\}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \phi\mu^{3}\]
In the dispersion parametrisation, \(\phi = 1/\lambda\) where \(\lambda\) is the shape used by some references. The variance function \(\phi\mu^{3}\) is what makes the inverse-square link canonical here (see Section 2.5.5).


3.1.16 Lognormal
lognormal_distrib()
Support: \(y \in (0, \infty)\).
\[f(y) = \frac{1}{y\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(\log y - \mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = e^{\mu + \sigma^{2}/2}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)e^{2\mu+\sigma^{2}}\]
\(\mu\) and \(\sigma^{2}\) are the mean and variance on the log scale, not of \(Y\) itself: dlnorm() takes sdlog, and this object takes its square. The same law can also be built as transformation(gaussian_distrib(), exp_transform()), by the change of variables of Section 3.2.1, and the two constructions coincide.


3.1.17 Beta
beta_distrib()
Support: \(y \in (0, 1)\).
\[f(y) = \frac{y^{a-1}(1-y)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}, \qquad a = \mu\phi, \quad b = (1-\mu)\phi\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \dfrac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}\]
The mean-precision parametrisation of beta regression, not the shape1/shape2 one: \(a = \mu\phi\), \(b = (1-\mu)\phi\), so \(a/(a+b) = \mu\) and \(a+b = \phi\). Larger \(\phi\) means less dispersion.


3.1.18 Bernoulli
bernoulli_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \{0, 1\}\).
\[P(Y=y) = \mu^{y}(1-\mu)^{1-y}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu(1-\mu)\]
Its support has two points, which is the whole content of Section 3.2.8: a Bernoulli has exactly one free probability, so neither zero-inflating nor zero-adjusting it produces an identified model.


3.1.19 Binomial
binomial_distrib(size = 10)
Support: \(y \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\).
\[P(Y=y) = \binom{n}{y}\mu^{y}(1-\mu)^{n-y}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = n\mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = n\mu(1-\mu)\]
The number of trials \(n\) is a property of the object, not a parameter: it is known, not estimated, so it belongs with size rather than in theta. Shown at \(n = 10\).


3.1.20 Poisson
poisson_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\).
\[P(Y=y) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{y}}{y!}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu\]
Equidispersed by construction, which is what makes it the natural parent for the zero-inflation and hurdle wrappers of Section 3.2: excess zeros are one of the two standard ways real count data depart from it.


3.1.21 Negative binomial (NB2)
negbin_distrib()
Support: \(y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\).
\[P(Y=y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!}\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{\theta}\left(\frac{\mu}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{y}\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu + \dfrac{\mu^{2}}{\theta}\]
The NB2 parametrisation: \(\theta\) is the size, and dispersion decreases as \(\theta\) grows, with the Poisson recovered as \(\theta \to \infty\). The excess kurtosis is \(6/\theta + \theta/(\mu(\theta+\mu))\). That expression is worth stating explicitly because the predecessor package this one replaces had \(6/\theta + (\theta+\mu)/(\mu\theta)\), which is wrong; it was found by numerical comparison, not by reading. Every formula inherited from that package was subsequently treated as unverified until checked.

title: 3  The distributions7 package
text:
3.1.1 The object and its contract
A distribution is an S7 object carrying its name, its dimensionality, the bounds of its support, the names and interpretations of its parameters, their individual domains, the link function attached to each of them, and a per-parameter flag recording whether the log-likelihood is differentiable in that parameter — a flag whose purpose will become clear in Section 3.1.22. Two subclasses, continuous_distrib and discrete_distrib, provide the defaults appropriate to each kind.

d <- gamma_distrib()
d@params
#> [1] "mu"     "sigma2"
d@params_bounds
#> $mu
#> [1]   0 Inf
#> 
#> $sigma2
#> [1]   0 Inf
d@link_params$sigma2
#> S7 Link Object: log
#>   - Parameter domain (theta): (0, Inf)

Parameters travel through the API as a named list called theta, and every generic normalises this list before doing anything else. The normalisation reorders the entries by name, so that list(sigma2 = 2, mu = 3) and list(mu = 3, sigma2 = 2) mean the same thing rather than silently meaning different things; it strips names from the values, because a parameter that has passed through a link function comes back carrying its own name, which would otherwise leak into the results and label a density "sigma2"; and it validates every value against the parameter’s domain.
The domains are treated as open intervals, and the openness is a deliberate choice rather than a pedantic one. A Gaussian requires \(\sigma > 0\), not \(\sigma \geq 0\), and a Bernoulli requires \(0 < \mu < 1\): at the closed boundary the log-likelihood and its derivatives cease to exist, and accepting the boundary value would only trade an informative error now for an unexplained NaN several calls later.

distrib_pdf(gaussian_distrib(), 1, list(mu = 0, sigma = 0))
#> Error:
#> ! Invalid parameter value(s) for the 'gaussian' distribution:
#>   'sigma' = 0 is outside its domain (0, Inf)

The generics fall into four natural groups:

The generics






Group
Generics




Probability
distrib_pdf, distrib_cdf, distrib_quantile, distrib_rng, distrib_atoms


Parameter derivatives
distrib_gradient, distrib_hessian, distrib_expected_hessian, distrib_deriv3, distrib_deriv4


Response derivatives
distrib_grad_y, distrib_hess_y


Moments
expectation, mean, variance, std_dev, skewness, kurtosis, moment



Of all of these, only distrib_pdf has no default; everything else can be derived from the density alone, as the Rayleigh example of Section 1.4 showed.


3.1.2 Score and information
Fix a distribution with density or mass function \(f(y;\theta)\), where \(\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_p)^\top\), and write \(\ell(\theta; y) = \log f(y;\theta)\) for the log-likelihood of a single observation. Derivatives with respect to the parameters are written with parenthesized superscripts,
\[
\ell^{(i)} = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_i}, \qquad
\ell^{(ij)} = \frac{\partial^{2} \ell}{\partial \theta_i \partial \theta_j}, \qquad
\ell^{(ijk)} = \frac{\partial^{3} \ell}{\partial \theta_i \partial \theta_j \partial \theta_k},
\]
and so on. The choice is deliberate. A subscript on \(\ell\) is left free for what subscripts usually mean in likelihood work — \(\ell_i\) as the contribution of the \(i\)-th observation, or, in the next chapter, \(\ell_Y\) as the log-likelihood of a transformed model — while the parenthesized superscript unambiguously marks a derivative, in the same spirit as \(f^{(k)}\) for the \(k\)-th derivative of a function of one variable. Indeed the two usages agree: when \(\ell\) depends on a single parameter \(\theta\), the \(k\)-th derivative can be written either as \(\ell^{(k)}\) with an integer order or as \(\ell^{(\theta\cdots\theta)}\) with the label repeated, and both forms appear below where each is the clearer one.
The vector \((\ell^{(1)}, \dots, \ell^{(p)})^\top\) is the score; the matrix \(-[\ell^{(ij)}]\) is the observed information; and the expected information, or Fisher information, is \(\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}]\), the expectation being taken over \(Y \sim f(\cdot\,;\theta)\) at the same parameter value.
A word on sign conventions, because both conventions circulate and a sign error here is invisible inside a symmetric matrix. The package returns derivatives, not informations: distrib_hessian() gives \([\ell^{(ij)}]\), and distrib_expected_hessian() gives \(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}]\), each with the sign of the derivative, so the informations are the negatives of what the functions return.
Since mixed partial derivatives are symmetric, only one representative of each multi-index is stored, and components are returned as named lists keyed in a canonical order — "mu_sigma2" stands for \(\ell^{(\mu\sigma^2)} = \ell^{(\sigma^2\mu)}\):

d <- gamma_distrib()
th <- list(mu = 3, sigma2 = 2)
y <- c(1, 2.5, 7)

str(distrib_gradient(d, y, th))
#> List of 2
#>  $ mu    : num [1:3] -1.9502 0.0487 0.8875
#>  $ sigma2: num [1:3] 0.713 -0.224 0.834
str(distrib_hessian(d, y, th))
#> List of 3
#>  $ mu_mu        : num [1:3] -1.722 -0.806 0.224
#>  $ sigma2_sigma2: num [1:3] -0.8468 0.0898 -0.9685
#>  $ mu_sigma2    : num [1:3] 1.154 0.155 -0.265

Everything in this section and the next two assumes the model is regular at \(\theta\): the support of \(f\) does not depend on \(\theta\), the log-likelihood is four times differentiable, and derivatives may be exchanged with the integral sign at the orders involved. Thirteen of the fourteen distributions in the catalogue satisfy these conditions everywhere; the exception is the Laplace, whose location parameter sits at a kink of the log-likelihood, and Section 3.1.22 is devoted to what happens then.


3.1.3 The Bartlett identities
Most readers will know the identity \(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}] = -\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)} \ell^{(j)}]\), the information matrix equality. What is less often written down is that this is only the second member of an infinite family of identities, one for each order of differentiation, and that the family taken as a whole allows an expected derivative of any order to be computed from expectations of products of lower-order ones. distributions7 implements the family in full generality, so this section derives it.
The starting point could hardly be simpler: a density integrates to one, and it does so for every value of the parameter,
\[\int f(y;\theta)\, dy = 1 \qquad \text{for all } \theta \in \Theta.\]
The right-hand side is constant in \(\theta\), so every derivative of the left-hand side must vanish, and regularity lets us take those derivatives under the integral sign:
\[\int \frac{\partial^{k} f}{\partial\theta_{i_1}\cdots\partial\theta_{i_k}}\,dy = 0.
\tag{3.1}\]
Everything now depends on expressing the derivatives of \(f\) through the derivatives of \(\ell = \log f\), and the expression turns out to have a beautiful combinatorial structure.

Lemma 3.1 (Derivatives of \(e^{\ell}\)) For every \(k \geq 1\),
\[
\frac{\partial^{k} e^{\ell}}{\partial\theta_{i_1}\cdots\partial\theta_{i_k}}
= e^{\ell} \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} \prod_{B \in \pi} \ell^{(B)} ,
\]
where \(\Pi_k\) is the set of all partitions of the index set \(\{i_1, \dots, i_k\}\) into non-empty blocks, and \(\ell^{(B)}\) is the derivative of \(\ell\) with respect to the parameters indexed by the block \(B\).


Proof. We argue by induction on \(k\). For \(k = 1\) the claim reads \(\partial_i e^{\ell} = e^{\ell}\ell^{(i)}\), which is the chain rule, and indeed \(\Pi_1\) contains the single partition \(\{\{i\}\}\).
Suppose the formula holds at order \(k\), and differentiate it with respect to a new index \(\theta_{i_{k+1}}\). By the product rule, the derivative acts either on the factor \(e^{\ell}\) in front — producing an extra factor \(\ell^{(i_{k+1})}\) — or on one of the factors \(\ell^{(B)}\) inside a partition, turning it into \(\ell^{(B \cup \{i_{k+1}\})}\). In the first case, the new index ends up in a block of its own; in the second, it joins an existing block. But these two cases are precisely the two ways of building a partition of the \((k{+}1)\)-element set from a partition of the \(k\)-element set, and every partition of the larger set arises in exactly one of the two ways, from exactly one partition of the smaller set. The sum therefore runs over \(\Pi_{k+1}\) with each term appearing once, which is the claim at order \(k+1\). \(\square\)

Substituting the lemma into (3.1), and noticing that \(e^{\ell} = f\) is exactly the density needed to turn the integral into an expectation, we arrive at the result.

Theorem 3.1 (Bartlett identities) Under the regularity conditions above, for every \(k \geq 1\) and every choice of indices,
\[\sum_{\pi \,\in\, \Pi_k} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\;\prod_{B \in \pi} \ell^{(B)} \right] = 0.\]

To use the identity, single out the partition consisting of one big block: its contribution is \(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i_1 \cdots i_k)}]\), the expected derivative of top order, and moving everything else to the other side,
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell^{(i_1\cdots i_k)}\right]
= -\sum_{\substack{\pi \in \Pi_k \\ |\pi| > 1}}
   \mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{B\in\pi}\ell^{(B)}\right].
\tag{3.2}\]
The first three cases, written out, show the family growing out of familiar ground:
\[
\begin{aligned}
k = 1: \quad & \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)}] = 0, \\[4pt]
k = 2: \quad & \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}] = -\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)}\ell^{(j)}], \\[4pt]
k = 3: \quad & \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ijk)}] = -\Big(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ij)}\ell^{(k)}]
   + \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(ik)}\ell^{(j)}] + \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(jk)}\ell^{(i)}]
   + \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)}\ell^{(j)}\ell^{(k)}]\Big).
\end{aligned}
\]
The case \(k = 1\) is the zero-mean property of the score; the case \(k = 2\) is the information matrix equality, and read from right to left it says that the outer-product-of-gradients estimator of the information is not a separate idea but the second Bartlett identity itself. The implementation follows the mathematics directly: it enumerates the set partitions of the index set and sums products of quantities the distribution already provides. The number of terms is the Bell number \(B_k\) — one, two, five and fifteen for \(k = 1, \dots, 4\) — so the computation stays small at every order the toolkit supports.

Three ways to take an expectation
When a distribution has no closed-form expected derivative, the expectation has to be approximated, and the derivative generics accept an approx argument choosing among three strategies. The strategy "bartlett" (also spelled "opg") applies (3.2); at second order it needs nothing but the score, which makes it the cheapest option, and it is the default there. The strategy "integrate" computes \(\mathbb{E}[\partial^k \ell]\) literally, by quadrature for continuous distributions and by summation for discrete ones; when the observed derivative is available in closed form this is usually the most accurate route, and it is the default at orders three and four. The strategy "mc" simulates from the distribution and averages the observed derivative over the draws; it is robust when quadrature struggles, at the price of Monte Carlo noise.
The difference between the first strategy and the other two is deeper than a matter of cost. "integrate" and "mc" estimate the expected derivative itself, whereas "bartlett" estimates the quantity that the identity says the expected derivative equals under regularity. When regularity fails, the two quantities part company, and the one that still deserves the name “information” is the Bartlett one — a point Section 3.1.22 makes concrete.






NoteA cautionary tale about quadrature



The expectation() engine splits its integral at quantiles of the distribution, and it uses three knots rather than nine. More knots would extend the range of densities it can integrate at all, but they would also convert loud failures into silent wrong answers: at Gamma shape \(0.02\), a nine-knot rule returns \(-54.9\) for a quantity that is exactly zero, while the three-knot rule simply reports that the integral could not be computed. In the ordinary range three knots are also the more accurate choice, since every extra panel contributes its own quadrature error. An error is worth more than a plausible number.





3.1.4 Derivatives on the link scale
The parameters of a distribution are constrained, and the linear predictors of a model are not, so every derivative generic accepts an argument scale = c("parameter", "link"). With scale = "link" the derivatives are taken with respect to
\[\eta_i = g_i(\theta_i), \qquad \theta_i = h_i(\eta_i), \qquad h_i = g_i^{-1},\]
where \(g_i\) is the link that the distribution carries for its \(i\)-th parameter. The structural fact on which the whole section rests is that each parameter has its own link and the map is applied coordinate by coordinate, so the Jacobian of \(\theta\) with respect to \(\eta\) is diagonal. Diagonality is what makes the general multivariate chain rule collapse into a product of univariate ones, and we now work this out in stages, starting with a single parameter.

One parameter
Composing \(\ell\) with \(h\) and differentiating repeatedly is the territory of Faà di Bruno’s formula, which organises the combinatorial explosion of the chain rule through the partial Bell polynomials \(B_{m,j}\).

Theorem 3.2 (Faà di Bruno) If \(\ell\) is \(m\) times differentiable in \(\theta\) and \(h\) is \(m\) times differentiable in \(\eta\), with \(\theta = h(\eta)\), then
\[
\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial\eta^{m}}\,\ell(h(\eta))
= \sum_{j=1}^{m} \ell^{(j)}(\theta)\;
  B_{m,j}\!\left(h', h'', \dots, h^{(m-j+1)}\right).
\]

For the orders the toolkit uses, the Bell polynomials are small enough to list in full,
\[
\begin{array}{llll}
B_{1,1} = h' \\
B_{2,1} = h'' & B_{2,2} = (h')^{2} \\
B_{3,1} = h''' & B_{3,2} = 3h'h'' & B_{3,3} = (h')^{3} \\
B_{4,1} = h'''' & B_{4,2} = 4h'h''' + 3(h'')^{2} & B_{4,3} = 6(h')^{2}h'' & B_{4,4} = (h')^{4}
\end{array}
\]
and substituting them into the theorem gives the four formulas that the package applies:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \eta} &= \ell^{(\theta)}\,h', \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial^{2} \ell}{\partial \eta^{2}} &= \ell^{(\theta\theta)}\,(h')^{2} + \ell^{(\theta)}\,h'', \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial^{3} \ell}{\partial \eta^{3}} &= \ell^{(\theta\theta\theta)}\,(h')^{3} + 3\,\ell^{(\theta\theta)}\,h'h'' + \ell^{(\theta)}\,h''', \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial^{4} \ell}{\partial \eta^{4}} &= \ell^{(\theta\theta\theta\theta)}\,(h')^{4} + 6\,\ell^{(\theta\theta\theta)}\,(h')^{2}h'' + \ell^{(\theta\theta)}\left(4h'h''' + 3(h'')^{2}\right) + \ell^{(\theta)}\,h''''.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two lines are easily checked by hand — the first is the chain rule, and the second follows from differentiating it as a product — and they exhibit the property that makes the whole construction generic: each link-scale derivative is a linear combination of the parameter-scale derivatives of order up to \(m\), with coefficients that depend only on the link. The transformation never needs to know which distribution it is transforming, which is why it can be written once, in the body of the generic, for all distributions at once.


Several parameters
With several parameters, a mixed derivative such as \(\partial^4 \ell / \partial\eta_a^2\,\partial\eta_b^2\) must be handled, and here diagonality earns its keep.

Proposition 3.1 (Faà di Bruno with a diagonal Jacobian) Let the multi-index involve the distinct parameters \(p_1, \dots, p_r\) with multiplicities \(m_1, \dots, m_r\), and let \(k = \sum_t m_t\). Then
\[
\frac{\partial^{k} \ell}{\partial \eta_{p_1}^{m_1} \cdots \partial \eta_{p_r}^{m_r}}
= \sum_{j_1=1}^{m_1} \cdots \sum_{j_r=1}^{m_r}
   \ell^{(p_1^{j_1} \cdots p_r^{j_r})}
   \prod_{t=1}^{r} B_{m_t, j_t}\!\left(h_{p_t}', h_{p_t}'', \dots\right),
\]
where \(\ell^{(p_1^{j_1}\cdots p_r^{j_r})}\) denotes the parameter-scale derivative taken \(j_t\) times with respect to \(\theta_{p_t}\).


Proof. The key observation is that \(\theta_{p_t} = h_{p_t}(\eta_{p_t})\) depends on its own linear predictor and on nothing else, so the operator \(\partial^{m_t}/\partial\eta_{p_t}^{m_t}\) sees \(\ell\) as a function of the single variable \(\theta_{p_t}\), all other parameters held fixed. We may therefore apply Theorem 3.2 in the variable \(\eta_{p_1}\) alone, obtaining
\[
\frac{\partial^{m_1}\ell}{\partial\eta_{p_1}^{m_1}}
= \sum_{j_1=1}^{m_1} \ell^{(p_1^{j_1})}\, B_{m_1,j_1}\!\left(h_{p_1}', \dots\right),
\]
in which the coefficients \(B_{m_1, j_1}\) involve only the derivatives of \(h_{p_1}\) and therefore behave as constants under differentiation with respect to any other linear predictor. Applying the theorem again in \(\eta_{p_2}\), then \(\eta_{p_3}\), and so on — the operators commute, acting as they do on disjoint variables — each application multiplies in its own Bell polynomial factor and deepens the sum by one index, and after \(r\) rounds the stated nested sum is reached. \(\square\)

Two special cases are worth extracting because they cover most of what happens in practice. A purely mixed second derivative across two different parameters involves \(m_1 = m_2 = 1\), each inner sum has a single term, and the formula collapses to a rescaling,
\[
\frac{\partial^{2}\ell}{\partial\eta_a \partial\eta_b} = \ell^{(ab)}\,h_a'\,h_b'
\qquad (a \neq b).
\]
And the number of terms in the general sum is \(\prod_t m_t\) — at most eight for the orders the toolkit supports — so the computation remains trivial even at fourth order.


The expected Hessian transforms more simply
For expected second derivatives something pleasant happens: the awkward first-order term drops out on its own.

Corollary 3.1 (Congruence) \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ell}{\partial\eta_a\partial\eta_b}\right]
= h_a'\,h_b'\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell^{(ab)}\right],\]
or in matrix form \(\mathbb{E}[H_\eta] = \operatorname{diag}(h')\,\mathbb{E}[H_\theta]\,\operatorname{diag}(h')\).


Proof. For \(a = b\), the univariate formula gives \(\partial^2\ell/\partial\eta_a^2 = \ell^{(aa)}(h_a')^2 + \ell^{(a)} h_a''\). Take expectations: the first Bartlett identity says \(\mathbb{E}[\ell^{(a)}] = 0\), so the second term vanishes and only the congruence term survives. For \(a \neq b\) there was no first-order term to begin with. \(\square\)

The corollary matters beyond elegance. A congruence transform of a positive semi-definite matrix is positive semi-definite, so the link-scale Fisher information inherits the definiteness of the parameter-scale one automatically. Had one instead transformed the observed Hessian and then averaged numerically, the \(\ell^{(a)} h_a''\) term would have survived and that guarantee would have been lost.


Where the transformation lives
The change of scale is implemented once, in the body of each derivative generic, between the dispatch and the return: a method always computes parameter-scale values, and the generic transforms them if scale = "link" was requested.
distrib_gradient <- S7::new_generic(
  "distrib_gradient", "distrib",
  function(distrib, y, theta, scale = c("parameter", "link"), ...) {
    ...
    res <- S7::S7_dispatch()                    # parameter scale, always
    if (scale == "link") to_link_scale(...) else res
  })
This placement has one visible consequence for users who write their own derivative methods: since S7 requires a method’s formal arguments to include the generic’s named arguments, such a method must declare scale = c("parameter", "link"), ... in its signature even though it never touches scale itself. Omitting the declaration makes dispatch fail.



3.1.5 Derivatives with respect to the response
Besides derivatives in the parameters, continuous distributions provide \(\partial\ell/\partial y\) and \(\partial^{2}\ell/\partial y^{2}\) through distrib_grad_y() and distrib_hess_y(); for a lattice variable there is nothing to differentiate, so discrete distributions have no such methods. These quantities feed quantile residuals and smoothness criteria further up the toolkit. The default implementation is a central finite difference of the log-density with a step that shrinks near the boundary of the support, so that \(y \pm \delta\) never leaves it.

d <- gamma_distrib()
th <- list(mu = 3, sigma2 = 2)
distrib_grad_y(d, c(1, 3, 6), th)
#> [1]  2.0000000 -0.3333333 -0.9166667
# closed form: with shape a = mu^2/sigma2 and rate b = mu/sigma2,
# dl/dy = (a - 1)/y - b
(3^2 / 2 - 1) / c(1, 3, 6) - 3 / 2
#> [1]  2.0000000 -0.3333333 -0.9166667



3.1.6 Derivatives of the distribution function
Everything so far has differentiated the density. There is a second family of derivatives that a modelling framework needs and that is almost never provided: those of the distribution function with respect to the parameters. The reason they matter is censoring. An observation known only to be at most \(q\) contributes \(\log F(q;\theta)\) to the log-likelihood rather than \(\log f(y;\theta)\); one known only to exceed \(q\) contributes \(\log\big(1 - F(q;\theta)\big)\); and an interval-censored one contributes \(\log\big(F(b;\theta) - F(a;\theta)\big)\). Without \(\partial F/\partial\theta\) none of these can be fitted by any method that uses a score, which rules out survival models, tobit models and every problem with a detection limit.
The mathematics is a single exchange of derivative and integral, and it is worth seeing how little it costs. The region of integration is \((-\infty, q]\), fixed, not depending on \(\theta\) — the same condition that made truncation a regular problem in Theorem 3.5 — so
\[
\frac{\partial F(q;\theta)}{\partial\theta_i}
= \int_{-\infty}^{q}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_i}\,\mathrm{d}y
= \int_{-\infty}^{q} f\,\ell^{(i)}\,\mathrm{d}y
= F(q)\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell^{(i)} \,\middle|\, Y \leq q\right],
\]
using \(\partial_i f = f\,\ell^{(i)}\) in the middle step and dividing by \(F(q)\) in the last to recognise the conditional density. So the gradient of the log distribution function is a partial mean of the score: \(\partial_i \log F(q) = \mathbb{E}[\ell^{(i)} \mid Y \le q]\).
The second order follows the same way, with Lemma 3.2 supplying the integrand:
\[
\frac{\partial^{2} F(q)}{\partial\theta_i\partial\theta_j}
= F(q)\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell^{(ij)} + \ell^{(i)}\ell^{(j)} \,\middle|\, Y \leq q\right],
\]
and the log scale from \(\partial_{ij}\log P = \partial_{ij}P/P - (\partial_iP/P)(\partial_jP/P)\).
Two things follow for the implementation, and they pull in opposite directions. For a discrete distribution the expectation is a finite sum over the support up to \(q\), so the identity is not an approximation at all and can be evaluated as it stands. For a continuous one it is an integral over a semi-infinite region, and evaluating it by quadrature is both slower and less accurate than simply differencing the distribution function, which for every family in the catalogue is an analytic expression. The package does each where it belongs.
Some families need neither. For a location-scale family, \(F(y) = G(z)\) with \(z = (y-\mu)/\sigma\), and differentiating the composition gives the whole set in terms of quantities the distribution already provides:
\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mu} = -f(y), \qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\sigma} = -z\,f(y), \qquad
\frac{\partial^{2} F}{\partial\mu^{2}} = f(y)\,\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y},
\]
and similarly for the remaining second derivatives. The first of these is worth pausing on: the sensitivity of the distribution function to a shift in location is minus the density at that point — obvious once seen, since shifting the distribution to the right by \(\mathrm{d}\mu\) removes exactly \(f(q)\,\mathrm{d}\mu\) of mass from below \(q\).

d <- gaussian_distrib()
th <- list(mu = 1.2, sigma = 1.7)
q <- c(0, 1.2, 3)

distrib_grad_cdf(d, q, th, log = FALSE)$mu
#> [1] -0.1829209 -0.2346719 -0.1339725
-dnorm(q, 1.2, 1.7)
#> [1] -0.1829209 -0.2346719 -0.1339725

Putting it to work on a censored sample takes one line per kind of observation:

set.seed(1)
y <- distrib_rng(d, 200, list(mu = 1, sigma = 2))
cens <- y > 2.5          # everything above 2.5 is only known to be above it
y[cens] <- 2.5

# the score in mu: ordinary observations contribute the usual score, censored
# ones the derivative of log(1 - F)
sum(distrib_gradient(d, y[!cens], th)$mu) +
  sum(distrib_grad_cdf(d, y[cens], th, lower.tail = FALSE, log = TRUE)$mu)
#> [1] -12.02472

An interval-censored observation is assembled from the unlogged derivatives at the two endpoints, \(\partial\log(F(b)-F(a)) = (\partial F(b) - \partial F(a))/(F(b)-F(a))\), which is why the generic offers log = FALSE as well.
